author: @therundownai
title_or_hook: Tufa Labs tufazip at the Large Text Compression Benchmark
summary: Tufa Labs' tufazip, verified at the benchmark with one correction. The post says a 163M-parameter Transformer compressed 1GB of Wikipedia and ranked second on the benchmark in September 2026. Verified this run: the benchmark's own table (updated Nov 19, 2026) lists tufazip v2 at 105,388,353 bytes total for enwik9 (100,958,324 payload + 4,430,029 decoder/weights), a 12-layer 163M-parameter Transformer; the size and model figures are exact. Correction: v2 currently ranks 13th overall, not second; second place was v1's position at its Sept 7, 2026 submission (105,979,069 bytes). The defensible superlative is best entry using a neural network as its sole predictor; everything above it mixes neural with hand-built models. Cost: about 7.3 days to compress and 7.5 days to decompress on two B200 GPUs; a research result, not a usable archiver. License: MIT stated for v1 (0.1.0); no license stated for the v2 entry.
metrics_or_datasets: tufazip v2 total 105,388,353 bytes for enwik9 (100,958,324 payload + 4,430,029 decoder/weights)
163M-parameter, 12-layer Transformer
v2 ranks 13th overall; v1 ranked 2nd at its Sept 7, 2026 submission (105,979,069 bytes)
About 0.843 bits per byte on enwik9
About 7.3 days to compress and 7.5 days to decompress on two B200 GPUs
License: MIT stated for v1; no license stated for v2
verdict: LEARN-ONLY (verified, high pattern value, no deployable use)
engine_training_value: Bits-per-byte on enwik9 (about 0.843) is summed cross-entropy: the benchmark is a pure next-token-prediction score, which is why a compressor result is a language-model result. For GSE it trains nothing directly (text, not game data), but the pattern (one frozen-ish predictor, arithmetic coding, honest total-cost accounting including the decoder) is the same accounting discipline the reasoning doctrine demands: count the whole system, not the payload.
provenance: Post by @therundownai, an AI-news aggregator (recreator); origin is Tufa Labs (researcher Tommy He) and Matt Mahoney's Large Text Compression Benchmark. Verified this run at the benchmark's own table (updated Nov 19, 2026) plus benchmark coverage.
